subject: business
title: Business Alive Investigative Study
level: Common brief for Higher and Ordinary Level; marked at the level you sit the written paper
keyDates: Term 2 of 5th Year (2025/26 cycle for the 2027 exam) — SEC issued the 2027 brief (NCCA guidelines say the brief issues in Term 2 of year one; the exact issue date was not found in the sources)
12 March 2027 — coursework must be completed and submitted to your class teacher (SEC 2027 brief)

After 12 March 2027 — teacher and principal sign the SEC Authentication Form P.2; the school submits your PDF to the SEC through the Schools Portal (file-naming instructions come in an annual SEC Schools Portal circular; exact portal dates TBC by SEC)
June 2027 — written paper worth the other 60% (300 marks); exact timetable date not taken from the sources
summary: The Business Alive Investigative Study is a report of no more than 1,500 words in which you research one question, in response to an SEC brief, and show your planning and reflection. For 2027 you investigate how a work practice that uses digital technology is impacting either employers or employees, supported by primary and/or secondary data. It is worth 200 marks (40%), is done mostly in your own time over roughly 20 hours, is submitted as a PDF, and your teacher must authenticate it as your own work.

stages.name: Stage 1: Getting started (about 2-3 hours)
stages.marksNote: Feeds Planning and the Introduction (20 marks) and sets up Overall Coherence (50 marks).

points: The 2027 brief opens with a statement adapted from the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment: digitalisation drives productivity growth through better process efficiency and product/service quality, and is disrupting traditional roles and changing the world of work.

The task itself is to investigate how a work practice that uses digital technology is impacting either employers or employees. Read the word 'either': you pick one side, you are not asked to cover both.

You must support the investigation with appropriate primary and/or secondary data. Primary data is what you collect yourself (surveys, interviews); secondary data is existing material (reports, articles, statistics).
A common brief is used for Higher and Ordinary Level, so the same task applies whichever paper you sit.

The NCCA guidelines suggest asking: what do I already know about the theme, what else would I like to know, how does it link to what I have learned in Business or to business around me, and how might I learn more?
Edco suggests a mind map or a class brain-dump to find the main topics, and looking for examples locally, nationally and internationally.
Use class discussion with your teacher at this stage; teachers may facilitate discussion of the brief but should only give general, non-directive feedback.
Decide where you will store your background research. This is where your investigative folder starts.
The SEC strongly encourages you to keep an investigative folder. It is a record of your thoughts, how they change, and relevant learning and support material.
You do not submit the folder. Only the report goes to the SEC, so any evidence of planning and reflection must appear in the report itself.
Paste links and note the date you accessed every source from day one so referencing is easy later.

The study draws mainly on the Unifying Strand skills and applies the cross-cutting themes of the specification. Edco lists them as including financial literacy, business and entrepreneurial thinking, ethics and sustainability, and digital transformation; check the specification for the exact wording.
Digital transformation and technology topics in your course are the natural background for this brief.

checklistCandidates: Read the 2027 brief in full, including the quoted statement and the task sentence.
Choose to focus on either employers or employees, not both.
Start an investigative folder and log each source with its link and date accessed.
Download the SEC cover page (.docx) so it is ready for page one.

stages.name: Stage 2: Developing a research question (about 1-2 hours)
stages.marksNote: Feeds the Introduction (20 marks) and the 'clear and probing question' part of the Planning descriptor.

points: Use your background research to find an aspect of the brief that interests you, then identify the main issues, problems or gaps in your knowledge.

Use SMART objectives, repeating them if needed, to shape the question. The NCCA prompts ask: is it specific and linked to the brief; can it be measured using a range of sources; is it achievable with information you can access; is it relevant to your learning and to real business; and can it be done in the time you have.

A strong question names one digital work practice (for example a specific tool or way of working) and one group (employers or employees). Narrowing it keeps the report within 1,500 words and the research achievable.

The top descriptor asks for a 'clear and probing' question underpinned by the relevance or importance of business locally, nationally and/or internationally. So your rationale should say why the question matters to business.
Discuss your proposed question with your teacher, who may use the NCCA prompt questions to help you refine it.
The question can change as you progress. If you change it, note that you did and why; this is useful evidence when you reflect on your planning.
Check that you can actually obtain data. If you cannot reach enough sources, narrow or rethink the question now.
Section 1 (Introduction, about 200 words) must state your research question and explain why you chose it.

checklistCandidates: Write one research question about one digital work practice and one group (employers or employees).
Test the question against each SMART letter and note any change you make.
Write one sentence on why the question matters to business locally, nationally or internationally.
Agree the question with your teacher in discussion.

stages.name: Stage 3: Developing a project plan (about 1-2 hours)
stages.marksNote: Feeds Planning evidence in the Introduction (20 marks), the Conclusion (30 marks) and Overall Coherence (50 marks), where evidence of planning and reflection should be clear throughout.

points: Your objectives, linked to your research question.
The main tasks, your role, the resources you need, a time schedule, and possible risks.
Ongoing monitoring and evaluation: what is working, what could be better, whether you are on schedule, whether to reconsider the question or find more sources, and what the limitations are.
The NCCA guidelines (Appendix Two) give a layout with the columns Objectives, My role, Resources, Time schedule, Possible risks, and a row for ongoing monitoring and evaluation. You can use it.

guide.h: The plan is not submitted but is marked through your report
points: You do not submit the project plan. You are expected to refer to it throughout the report, reflecting on and evaluating how far your planning helped you finish the study.
The Introduction must reflect on how you engaged with your project plan; the Conclusion must outline how your planning contributed to the successful completion of the study.

The top Planning descriptor asks for effective engagement with planning throughout and clear reflection on and evaluation of its contribution. Writing 'I made a plan' is not enough; say what changed and what it did to the outcome.
Revisit the plan regularly and keep dated notes of problems and how you solved them.
Sharing your plan with your teacher is an important step in the ongoing authentication process.

checklistCandidates: Complete a plan with objectives, tasks, resources, time schedule and risks.
Update the plan at set points and log what changed and why.
Share the plan with your teacher.
Note two or three real planning decisions to reflect on in the Introduction and Conclusion.

stages.name: Stage 4 and 5: Sources, data, analysis and evaluation (about 6-8 hours combined)
stages.marksNote: Feeds Investigation, Findings, Analysis and Evaluation (100 marks, the largest block) and Overall Coherence (50 marks).

points: Gather evidence from a variety of primary and/or secondary sources: internet, print and online media, reports, commentary from people in business, surveys, interviews.
Choose sources most relevant to your question and make sure they give different perspectives. The brief tells you to consider a variety of perspectives in Section 2.
The top Investigating descriptor asks you to identify and evaluate the potential value of a wide range of appropriate sources, and to justify the choice of sources.
Record every source as you go, with the date accessed, key information, why it matters to your question, and your own reflection. The NCCA guidelines (Appendix Three) provide this layout.

Do your research in a responsible, safe and ethical way. Teachers must remind you to follow relevant rules on health and safety, GDPR and access to public or private property. Be careful with anything involving other people's personal data if you run a survey or interview.

The NCCA prompts: how relevant is it to my question; is it reliable and how do I know; how recent is it; is it biased and what is its purpose; is it fact or opinion; are there alternative explanations or perspectives?
Edco adds the checks: is the source credible, reliable, possibly biased, do I need more information, when was it written?
Say in the report why each type of source or method suits your question (Section 2: explain the purpose and relevance of the research methods and sources used).
Break the data into parts, look for patterns, trends and contradictions, and highlight what matters most for your question.
The top descriptor asks for in-depth analysis and evaluation of data from a range of reliable sources.
Section 3 (Analysis and Evaluation, about 600 words) is where the brief asks you to demonstrate originality and critical thinking. It is the biggest section, so spend your best words here.
Keep the facts you found separate from your interpretation of them, and always link findings back to the research question.
Present findings in appropriate formats. Charts, tables and graphs may be created by you or captured from a secondary source and embedded.
Do not use images to carry extra text. The total number of images allowed in the whole report is ten.
Any image you refer to in the body must be labelled (Figure 1, Figure 2 and so on).

Words in references, data tables, graphs, diagrams, images and labels do not count towards the 1,500-word limit, but the brief warns that marks fall if the report loses coherence through unwarranted length or too many images.

The top descriptor asks you to clearly identify limitations across the design of the question, the research you gathered and/or the analysis. Moderate achievement identifies some limitations; low achievement does not identify them.
Typical limitations to consider: small or unrepresentative sample, one business or one sector only, bias in a source, data being out of date, a narrow question.
Teachers can ask to see your work at regular intervals, so keep findings and analysis ready to share. Sharing this work is a step in ongoing authentication.

checklistCandidates: Use at least two different kinds of source and more than one perspective.
Log every source with link or details and date accessed as you use it.
Write one sentence per source or method saying why you chose it and how reliable it is.
Analyse the data for patterns, trends and contradictions, and relate each point to the research question.
State at least one limitation each in your question, data and analysis.
Label every image as a Figure and refer to it in the text; use ten images or fewer.

stages.name: Stage 6: Applying learning and drawing conclusions (about 1-2 hours)
stages.marksNote: Feeds the Conclusion (30 marks) and the Applying descriptor; also Overall Coherence (50 marks).

points: Section 4 is about 300 words. The brief asks for conclusions justified by the analysis and evaluation.
Outline how your planning contributed to the successful completion of the study.
Discuss how your perspective evolved as a result of the study.
Consider how your findings connect to the real world of business.

guide.h: Applying to the world of business
points: The NCCA prompts: how do the findings answer my question and my objectives; how do they relate to what I learned across the Business course; how can they be applied to business locally, nationally or internationally; how do they link to business stories in the media; how do they link to the cross-cutting themes; how have they influenced my perspective?

The top Applying descriptor asks you to clearly and appropriately relate your findings to the cross-cutting theme(s) and to reflect on how the findings relate to business, and to business-related stories in the media where relevant.
Name the cross-cutting theme you are linking to (digital transformation is the obvious one for this brief) and explain the link rather than just listing it.
Identify what succeeded, what was a challenge, and what you changed in your plan.
Be honest. The NCCA guidelines say your report should be an authentic account of the investigative process.

checklistCandidates: Answer the research question directly, using only conclusions your analysis supports.
State how your planning helped, with one specific example.
State how your perspective changed.
Link findings to a real business, a media story or a cross-cutting theme.

stages.name: Compiling, formatting and submitting the report (about 2-3 hours, due 12 March 2027)
stages.marksNote: Feeds Overall Coherence (50 marks: organisation, clarity, cohesion, logical structure, expression, originality, business terminology, accurate references) and the Communicating descriptor.

points: Use these headings, each beginning on a new page: 1. Introduction (about 200 words); 2. Investigation and Findings (about 400 words); 3. Analysis and Evaluation (about 600 words); 4. Conclusions (about 300 words); 5. References.
The maximum is 1,500 words. The suggested counts add to 1,500. The brief says the counts are suggested, but going over the prescribed total may cost marks.
Not counted towards the limit: words in references, data tables, graphs, diagrams, images, or labels.
The brief rewards 'skilful brevity'. Fewer marks are awarded if coherence is lost through unwarranted length or excessive images.
Section headings: Arial, black, size 14, bold.
Body text: Arial, black, size 12, 1.5 line spacing.
Allowed: bold, italics, numbering and bullets. Not allowed: coloured text, highlighted text, other fonts.
Portrait only. Page numbers at bottom-centre. Margins 20 mm on all four sides, and nothing in the margins because it may not be visible to examiners.
Complete the SEC cover page (.docx, downloadable from the SEC site) and make it the first page of your document.
The SEC provides no template or submission booklet. Structuring and formatting the document is your responsibility.
Record the sources of all the information you gathered. Use in-text citations that link to an entry in the reference list.

No particular referencing style is required, but there must be enough accurate detail for the reader to verify the source. For print: author, title, year and page or chapter. For online: the hyperlink and the date read or downloaded.
Be as specific as needed, for example page number, website section or a timestamp for a video or podcast.
The reference section is not counted in the word limit.
Convert the final report to PDF, print the PDF and proof-read it. Anything not visible on the printed copy will not be visible to examiners and cannot earn marks.
Give the digital version to your class teacher. An SEC Schools Portal circular each year explains how to name the PDF file; ask your teacher.
Keep a backup copy of your digital report and update it regularly.

Sign the SEC Authentication Form P.2; your teacher and the school principal also sign. The school keeps digital and printed copies until the appeals process finishes and submits the report to the SEC through the Schools Portal.
Teachers should not correct your report for redrafting. Feedback must be general and non-directive; teachers must not edit draft work or give model text.

checklistCandidates: Use the five SEC headings and start each on a new page.
Keep body text within 1,500 words using the 200/400/600/300 budget.
Format in Arial, size 12 for body and size 14 bold for headings, 1.5 spacing, black text, 20 mm margins, portrait, page numbers bottom-centre.
Put the completed SEC cover page first.
Check every in-text citation matches a reference entry, and references include link and date accessed.
Convert to PDF, print and proof-read the PDF before giving it to your teacher by 12 March 2027.
Sign the Authentication Form P.2 when your teacher gives it to you.

criteria.name: Introduction (SEC mark allocation)
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: A clearly stated research question, a rationale that explains why the question matters, and reflection on how you engaged with your project plan. The brief lists these three bullets for the section.

criteria.name: Investigation, Findings, Analysis and Evaluation (SEC mark allocation)
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: A wide range of appropriate sources whose value is evaluated and whose selection is justified; findings presented clearly in suitable formats with a variety of perspectives; in-depth analysis and evaluation of data from reliable sources; originality and critical thinking; limitations clearly identified across the question, research and analysis. The 100 marks cover Sections 2 and 3 together.

criteria.name: Conclusion (SEC mark allocation)
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: Conclusions justified by the analysis and evaluation; how planning contributed to completing the study; how your perspective evolved; real-world business connection, including the cross-cutting theme(s) and media stories where relevant.

criteria.name: Overall Coherence (SEC mark allocation; not a separate section)
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: Awarded for the whole report: organisation, clarity and cohesion, evidence of planning and reflection throughout, logical structure, clear expression, originality, effective use of business terminology and accurate references.

criteria.name: Descriptor: Planning (NCCA)
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: Effective engagement with planning throughout, with clear reflection on and evaluation of how far it contributed to completing the study; a clear and probing research question underpinned by the relevance or importance of business locally, nationally and/or internationally.

criteria.name: Descriptor: Investigating (NCCA)
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: Identifies and evaluates the potential value of a wide range of appropriate sources; in-depth analysis and evaluation of data from reliable sources, justifying their choice; conclusions justified by analysis; limitations clearly identified across question design, research and analysis.

criteria.name: Descriptor: Applying (NCCA)
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: Reflects on how findings relate to the world of business and to business stories in the media where relevant, and on how your perspective was influenced; clearly and appropriately relates findings to the cross-cutting theme(s).

criteria.name: Descriptor: Communicating (NCCA)
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: Clear and appropriate data, information and analysis using a range of relevant graphics; coherent and consistent language throughout; clearly acknowledged supporting references and reflections on the study.

rules: Maximum 1,500 words of report text; going over may lose marks. References, data tables, graphs, diagrams, images and labels are not counted.
Maximum 10 images in the whole report. Images must not be used to add extra text, and any image referred to in the body must be labelled (Figure 1, Figure 2 and so on).
Use the five SEC section headings; each section starts on a new page; headings Arial black 14 bold; body Arial black 12 with 1.5 spacing.
Black text only, no highlighting, no other fonts; bold, italics, numbering and bullets are allowed.
Portrait orientation, page numbers bottom-centre, 20 mm margins on all sides, and nothing in the margins.
The SEC cover page (.docx) must be completed and be the first page.
Submit as a PDF. Print and proof-read the PDF; anything not visible in print will not earn marks.
Complete the work and give it to your class teacher by 12 March 2027.
The work must be your own individual work. You, your teacher and the school principal sign the SEC Authentication Form P.2.

Reference every source you use. Including material not created by you and not properly referenced is plagiarism, treated as cheating, and investigated by the SEC under its Coursework Rules and Procedures.

Any use of AI must be acknowledged. The reference gives the tool name, the date, and a short explanation of how it was used; include the share URL if the tool provides one, otherwise the tool name and the prompt used. Material generated by AI and not acknowledged is plagiarism.
Penalties for submitting work not entirely your own can go up to withholding of related results.

Teachers may give general, non-directive feedback but must not edit draft work, correct the report for redrafting, or supply model text. Where classmates work on similar questions, each student must take an individual approach.
Do not submit your investigative folder or project plan; only the report is marked.
Research must be responsible, safe and ethical, following health and safety, GDPR and rules on access to property.
mistakes: Going over 1,500 words, or reaching the limit by shrinking writing into images or labels. The brief says images must not be used to carry extra text.
Using more than 10 images, or using images that are not referred to or labelled.
Describing your plan ('I made a plan') without reflecting on how it helped or changed. Planning and reflection should be evident throughout.
A broad question that tries to cover digital technology in general, or both employers and employees, instead of one practice and one group.
Relying on one source or one perspective, or not explaining why each source was chosen and whether it is reliable.
Describing data without analysis or evaluation, or reaching conclusions the data cannot support.
Leaving out limitations. The descriptors place 'does not identify limitations' at the lowest level.
Conclusions that do not link to the real world of business or the cross-cutting themes, or that skip how your perspective changed.
Inaccurate or incomplete references, missing access dates or links, or not acknowledging AI use.
Ignoring formatting rules (wrong font or spacing, coloured text, text in the margins), or not checking the printed PDF before submitting.
Leaving the report until late and not keeping the investigative folder, so the evidence of planning and monitoring is missing from the report.

conflicts: Section structure: the app (ch0-s4) says the report has five sections, with section two covering the project plan, risk assessment and monitoring and section three covering findings with source credibility. The SEC 2027 brief lists Introduction (about 200), Investigation and Findings (about 400), Analysis and Evaluation (about 600), Conclusions (about 300) and References. There is no separate project-plan section; planning is reflected on in the Introduction and Conclusion. I believe the SEC brief; the app should be corrected.

The app says the 'SMART refinement' sits in section one and that section five contains recommendations for a named audience. The SEC brief does not require either; the Introduction states the question and rationale, and the Conclusion covers justified conclusions, planning, perspective and real-world links. I believe the SEC brief.

Mark split: the app says only '40% / 200 marks' and tells students to 'check the brief'. The SEC brief now gives the split: Introduction 20, Investigation/Findings/Analysis/Evaluation 100, Conclusion 30, Overall Coherence 50. The app should add this.
Word-count rules: the app tells students to confirm what counts towards the limit. The SEC brief says references, data tables, graphs, diagrams, images and labels are excluded.

Timeline: Edco's guide says the report is submitted in term one of sixth year. The SEC brief says 12 March 2027 (Term 2 of 6th year) for completion and submission to the teacher. I believe the SEC brief, which is the current official source; the Edco guide was published in 2025 before the brief.

The app lists 'remote working, cloud collaboration and automation' as example practices and says the study 'asks students to investigate a digital work practice'. The SEC brief gives no examples and requires a work practice that uses digital technology, impacting either employers or employees. The examples are acceptable as illustration, but the app should say 'either employers or employees'.

The app says AI-generated work presented as your own breaches authentication rules. The SEC brief and NCCA guidelines allow research including AI but require any AI use to be acknowledged in references (tool, date, how used, share URL or prompt); unacknowledged AI material is plagiarism. The app should say this.

The app says the 'investigative folder' holds the dated monitoring entries and implies it is assessed. The SEC brief says the folder is encouraged but not submitted, so planning evidence must appear in the report.
Formatting rules (Arial, size 12, 1.5 spacing, 20 mm margins, portrait, page numbers, cover page, PDF) are in the SEC brief but not in the app.

Unconfirmed: the brief's issue date in Term 2 of 5th Year and the SEC Schools Portal file-naming circular were not found in the sources, and the 2027 written exam date was not checked. Studyclix and Examly pages would not load, so only their search snippets were used.
